title: The Haunter of the Dark by H. P. Lovecraft

evidence.paraphrase: The framing narrator presents a rational/skeptical explanation for Blake's death as the common belief.
evidence.quote:
Cautious investigators will hesitate to challenge the common belief
that Robert Blake was killed by lightning, or by some profound nervous
shock derived from an electrical discharge.

evidence.paraphrase: The narrator explicitly contrasts a skeptical, materialist account with the supernatural interpretation, inviting reader judgment.
evidence.quote:
Between these two schools of opinion the reader must judge for himself.
The papers have given the tangible details from a skeptical angle,
leaving for others the drawing of the picture as Robert Blake saw
it\u2014or thought he saw it\u2014or pretended to see it.

evidence.paraphrase: The narrator frames the account as a close, dispassionate study of documentary evidence (the diary).
evidence.quote:
Now, studying the
diary closely, dispassionately, and at leisure, let us summarize the
dark chain of events from the expressed point of view of their chief
actor.

evidence.paraphrase: Blake systematically researches books, newspaper files, and works to decipher a cryptogram.
evidence.quote:
During the days which followed, Blake told no one of his expedition.
Instead, he read much in certain books, examined long years of
newspaper files downtown, and worked feverishly at the cryptogram in
that leather volume from the cobwebbed vestry room.

evidence.paraphrase: Blake methodically eliminates possible languages while attempting to crack the cryptogram.
evidence.quote:
The cipher, he soon
saw, was no simple one; and after a long period of endeavor he felt
sure that its language could not be English, Latin, Greek, French,
Spanish, Italian, or German.

evidence.paraphrase: Blake decodes the cipher and identifies the language as the invented Aklo tongue of ancient cults.
evidence.quote:
It was in June that Blake's diary told of his victory over the
cryptogram. The text was, he found, in the dark Aklo language used by
certain cults of evil antiquity

evidence.paraphrase: The stone is explained as a device functioning as a window onto all time and space, with an origin on Yuggoth.
evidence.quote:
Of the Shining Trapezohedron he speaks often, calling it a window
on all time and space, and tracing its history from the days it was
fashioned on dark Yuggoth, before ever the Old Ones brought it to
earth.

evidence.paraphrase: A long history spanning eons and distant places/beings is traced for the artifact.
evidence.quote:
It was treasured and placed in its curious box by the crinoid
things of Antarctica, salvaged from their ruins by the serpent-men of
Valusia, and peered at eons later in Lemuria by the first human beings.
It crossed strange lands and stranger seas, and sank with Atlantis

evidence.paraphrase: The diary explains a rule: the entity is awakened by gazing into the stone.
evidence.quote:
There are references to a Haunter of the Dark awaked by
gazing into the Shining Trapezohedron, and insane conjectures about the
black gulfs of chaos from which it was called.

evidence.paraphrase: A stated operating principle: the entity cannot exist in light, flees weak light, is banished by strong light, and must be re-summoned.
evidence.quote:
Fr. O'Malley tells of devil-worship with box found in great Egyptian
ruins\u2014says they call up something that can't exist in light. Flees a
little light, and banished by strong light. Then has to be summoned
again.

evidence.paraphrase: After Blake enters the church, new disturbances begin in the steeple, changing conditions in the neighborhood.
evidence.quote:
It appears that a new fear had been
growing on Federal Hill since a stranger had entered the dreaded
church. The Italians whispered of unaccustomed stirrings and bumpings
and scrapings in the dark windowless steeple

evidence.paraphrase: A power outage leads to the entity emerging, following the established rule that darkness frees it.
evidence.quote:
Those living near the dreaded church had sworn that the thing
in the steeple had taken advantage of the street lamps' absence and
gone down into the body of the church, flopping and bumping around in
a viscous, altogether dreadful way.

evidence.paraphrase: Blake reacts with extreme horror to the news reports.
evidence.quote:
Then something in the Journal on the morning of July 17 threw the
diarist into a veritable fever of horror.

evidence.paraphrase: Blake frantically contacts the power company fearing a blackout, showing mounting terror.
evidence.quote:
It has been verified that on three
occasions\u2014during thunderstorms\u2014he telephoned the electric light
company in a frantic vein and asked that desperate precautions against
a lapse of power be taken.

evidence.paraphrase: The narrator offers a natural-causes framing against the supernatural interpretation of events at the church.
evidence.quote:
Of course there was nothing which can be proved
as being outside the order of nature. The possible causes of such an
event are many.

evidence.paraphrase: Naturalistic chemical/physical explanations are proposed for the church phenomena.
evidence.quote:
Mephitic vapors\u2014spontaneous
combustion\u2014pressure of gases born of long decay\u2014any one of numberless
phenomena might be responsible.

evidence.paraphrase: A violent event occurs as the tower louver-boarding breaks and crashes down.
evidence.quote:
Then at last there was a sound of splintering wood, and
a large, heavy object crashed down in the yard beneath the frowning
easterly fa\u00e7ade.

evidence.paraphrase: The entity's release produces a violent wind and disturbance affecting the crowd.
evidence.quote:
At the same time the
air trembled with a vibration as of flapping wings, and a sudden
east-blowing wind more violent than any previous blast snatched off the
hats and wrenched the dripping umbrellas of the crowd.

evidence.paraphrase: The official verdict attributes Blake's death to electrical shock, contrasting the supernatural account.
evidence.quote:
Shortly afterward the coroner's physician made an examination,
and despite the unbroken window reported electrical shock, or nervous
tension induced by an electrical discharge, as the cause of death.

evidence.paraphrase: Blake speculates in scientific terms about radioactivity/phosphorescence of the glowing stone.
evidence.quote: Was there a subtle phosphorescence of radio-activity about the thing?

evidence.paraphrase: Blake experiences sudden panic and senses an alien presence near the stone.
evidence.quote:
Then all at once the spell was broken by an access of gnawing,
indeterminate panic fear. Blake choked and turned away from the stone,
conscious of some formless alien presence close to him

evidence.paraphrase: As a consequence of the rapport, Blake begins sleepwalking toward the church, drawn by the entity.
evidence.quote:
There is mention of a night when he awaked to find
himself fully dressed, outdoors, and headed automatically down College
Hill toward the west. Again and again he dwells on the fact that the
thing in the steeple knows where to find him.

evidence.paraphrase: Blake reports collapse of spatial distance, perceiving the distant tower as if near.
evidence.quote:
Sense of distance gone\u2014far is near and near is far. No light\u2014no
glass\u2014see that steeple\u2014that tower\u2014window\u2014can hear

evidence.paraphrase: Blake's body shows an expression of extreme fright, and witnesses recoil.
evidence.quote:
the intruders saw the glassy, bulging eyes, and the marks of stark,
convulsive fright on the twisted features, they turned away in sickened
dismay.
